title: What Is a Buzz Cut? Guard Numbers, Styles and How to Cut It

description: A buzz cut is hair clipped to one short, even length with a guard, usually #1 to #4 (3 to 13 mm). Guard chart, every buzz cut type and a home method.
dek: A buzz cut is hair clipped to one short, even length with a guard, usually #1 to #4 (3 to 13 mm).
intro: A buzz cut is a haircut where the hair is clipped to one short, even length all over the head with electric clippers and a numbered guard, most often a #1 to #4, which leaves about 3 to 13 millimeters. Barbers generally call anything cut with a single guard at #4 or shorter a buzz.

It is the simplest haircut there is, and still easy to get wrong. Go one guard too short and your scalp shows under bright light; go one too long and it reads as a grown-out cut rather than a choice. This guide covers what each guard number leaves, every type of buzz cut, how to tell if one suits you, and how to cut, fade and maintain it at home.
quickAnswer: A buzz cut means cutting all of your hair to the same short length with clippers. A #2 guard (about 1/4 inch or 6 mm) is the classic buzz, a #1 (3 mm) is sharper, and a #3 or #4 (10 to 13 mm) is softer. If it is your first one, start with a #3 and step down later.

sections.h: What Is a Buzz Cut? Guard Numbers, Styles and How to Cut One at a Glance

blocks.p: **Short answer:** a buzz cut is hair cut to one uniform short length with clippers, usually with a #1 to #4 guard. The guard number sets the length, and the length sets the look.

blocks.h3: What barbers count as a buzz cut

blocks.p: To most barbers, a buzz cut is any style done with clippers and guards rather than scissors, where the top is #4 or shorter. A cut that is all one length, the same level everywhere, is the purest version. Once the top gets longer than about half an inch and the sides are tapered shorter, most barbers call it a crew cut or a short crop instead.

A buzz takes about ten minutes, needs no styling product, dries instantly and costs almost nothing to maintain once you own clippers. The trade-off is that your head shape, scalp and hairline become the hairstyle, so picking the right length matters more than with any other cut.

sections.h: What Do Buzz Cut Guard Numbers Mean?

blocks.p: On most American clippers, guards are numbered in eighths of an inch. A #1 leaves about 1/8 inch, a #2 about 1/4 inch, a #4 about 1/2 inch and a #8 a full inch. In metric, each full step is roughly 3 mm, with a few uneven jumps. Wahl, Andis and Oster use the same basic system, but lengths can differ by a millimeter between brands, so stick with one brand's guards for consistent results.

Below #1 sit the half sizes. A #0.5 leaves about 1.5 mm and a #1.5 about 4.5 mm, which is handy for blending. With no guard, most clippers cut about 0.5 to 1 mm with the taper lever closed and closer to 2 to 3 mm with it open. Foil shavers go down to bare skin.

blocks.h3: Why the same number looks different on different heads

blocks.p: Hair lies down as it grows, so a 6 mm cut does not look like 6 mm of standing hair. Coarse, straight hair stands up and looks longer and fuller. Fine or curly hair lies flatter and shows more scalp. Treat the chart as a starting point and adjust one guard after you see the result.

sections.h: What Are the Different Types of Buzz Cut?

blocks.p: There are six common types of buzz cut, plus a finishing touch that works on all of them.
No guard at all, the whole head at the clipper's closest setting. It is the recruit look: very clean and bold, and it shows every bump and scar.
A uniform #1 or #2, just enough hair to give the head color. This is the most common buzz and what most people mean when they say buzz cut.
A uniform #3 or #4, long enough to show texture and soften the outline of the head. It suits men who want a buzz without a shaved look.
Longer on top, often #4 to #6, with shorter tapered sides and back. It sits right at the edge of buzz territory and is more forgiving of head shape. Two guard sizes are all you need.
Very short or skin on the sides and back almost to the top of the head, with a short #1 to #3 strip on top. A strong military look that needs weekly upkeep.
Any uniform top length with the sides graduated shorter toward the ears and neck. It sharpens the shape and makes a home cut look barber-finished.

Squaring off the hairline at the forehead, temples and neck with a trimmer. It works on any style, but go easy at the front: pushing the line back to straighten it makes a receding hairline more obvious as it grows.

sections.h: Should You Get a Buzz Cut? How to Pick a Length

blocks.p: Yes, if you want a low-effort cut and your head shape and scalp hold up at short lengths. The safe way to find out is to start one or two guards longer than you think you want. Going shorter takes a minute; going back up takes two to three weeks of regrowth.
A #3 looks deliberate on almost everyone, hides most scalp scars and birthmarks, and grows out without an awkward stage. Live with it for a few days. If you like it, use a #2 next time.

blocks.h3: Hair color changes how short you can go

blocks.p: Dark hair on light skin gives strong contrast, so even a #1 reads as a solid, intentional cut. Blond, gray or very light hair shows more scalp at the same length and can look patchy below a #2. Dark hair on darker skin shows little contrast, so very short cuts look clean and even.

Thick, coarse hair stands up and looks full at any length, so it suits short buzzes. Fine hair looks best either very short, where hair and scalp blend, or at #3 to #4, where length hides gaps. The in-between lengths show thinning most.

Short cuts are cooler in summer, fit under helmets and dry instantly after a workout or swim. They also leave your scalp exposed to sun and cold, so at #2 and shorter, plan on a hat or scalp sunscreen if you spend hours outdoors.

sections.h: Does a Buzz Cut Suit Your Head Shape and Face?

blocks.p: A buzz cut removes the hair that normally rounds off the head, so head shape matters more than face shape. Run a hand over the back and crown, and check your profile using two mirrors.
A flat back of the head, a ridge or an uneven crown shows more at #1 than at #3. A crew cut, with a slightly longer top and shorter sides, balances a flat back or narrow crown.

Strong jaws and square or oval faces suit very short buzzes because the hair does not compete with the bone structure. Round faces often look better with a fade that keeps the sides tight and adds angles through contrast. Long faces do better with slightly fuller sides rather than a skin fade, which keeps the head from looking taller.

A short beard or heavy stubble adds weight to the lower face and balances a short buzz, especially on rounder faces. Blend the sideburns into the beard with a guard one size longer than the head so there is no hard line at the ear. Clean-shaven? A slightly longer buzz softens the look.

Check your hairline under bright overhead light. A widow's peak or deep temple recession is obvious at #1 and nearly invisible at #3. If you add a line-up, follow your natural hairline and never take the front line back further than it already sits.

sections.h: Is a Buzz Cut Good for Thinning Hair?

blocks.p: Yes. A short buzz is one of the best cuts for thinning hair. With longer hair, thin areas show as gaps between strands and a contrast between full sides and a sparse crown. Cut everything short and the density difference shrinks, so the eye reads one even shape.

Mild thinning at the crown often looks best at #2 or #3. Visible thinning across the top usually looks best at #1 or #0.5. When the top is mostly bare, many men shave the whole head, which looks cleaner than a short fringe around the sides.

blocks.h3: Keep the sides no longer than the top

blocks.p: Leaving fuller sides to compensate actually draws attention to a thin top. Match lengths, or fade the sides shorter, so the top looks relatively fuller.

blocks.h3: Treatments are easier with short hair

blocks.p: If you use a hair loss treatment such as minoxidil, short hair makes it easier to apply and lets it reach the scalp. Talk to a doctor or dermatologist about any treatment, especially prescription options. Short hair also makes it easier to judge progress over months.

sections.h: What Do You Need to Give Yourself a Buzz Cut?

blocks.p: You need a clipper with a full guard set, a trimmer for the edges, a way to see the back of your head and a plan for cleanup. A decent home kit pays for itself within a few cuts.

Look for a strong motor, guards from #0.5 to #8 and a taper lever for half-step adjustments. Corded clippers with magnetic or pivot motors, such as long-running Wahl and Andis models, are reliable and never die mid-cut. Cordless clippers make the back of the head easier to reach; choose a lithium-ion model that runs at least an hour per charge.

Thin plastic guards flex in thick hair and cut shorter on some passes than others. Sturdier guards, or guards with metal clips, hold length better. Use guards made for your clipper, because universal guards can sit unevenly on the blade.

A T-blade trimmer is narrower and cuts closer than a clipper for the hairline, neck and ears. A three-way mirror, a hand mirror or a phone recording the back solves the visibility problem. Clipper oil, a cleaning brush and a blade disinfectant spray keep the blades sharp and clean.

Clipped hair gets everywhere, so cut in a bathroom or on a hard floor rather than carpet. Tile, [vinyl plank flooring](/best-vinyl-plank-flooring/) and [laminate](/best-laminate-flooring/) sweep clean in a minute, and a small wet-dry vac from our [shop vac picks](/best-shop-vac/) pulls up the fine stubble a broom pushes around. A cape or old towel keeps hair off your clothes.

sections.h: How Do You Cut a Buzz Cut at Home?

blocks.p: Use clean, dry hair, cut against the grain in slow overlapping passes, work in a fixed order and finish the edges with a trimmer.

Wash and fully dry your hair; wet hair clumps and cuts unevenly, and some clippers are not built for wet use. Comb it so it stands away from the scalp. Put a few drops of oil on the blade, run it for a few seconds and wipe off the excess. Snap the guard on and check it is firmly seated.

On most heads that means nape up to crown at the back, bottom of the sides up toward the top, and forehead back over the top. Keep the guard flat on the scalp with light pressure and move slowly. Cover every area twice from different directions, because hair swirls around the crown.

blocks.h3: Step 3: Work in order and check

blocks.p: Go top, right side, left side, then back. Check the back with a mirror or phone video, then run a hand over your head: longer hairs stand out by feel even when you cannot see them. Go over those spots again with the same guard.

Remove the guard or switch to the trimmer to tidy around the ears and neckline. A tapered neckline grows out most naturally; rounded and squared lines need more upkeep. Stay at or below the natural hairline.
Brush hair out of the blade and guard, spray with disinfectant and oil the blade before storing. A clean, oiled blade cuts smoother and lasts far longer.

sections.h: How Do You Add a Fade to a Buzz Cut?

blocks.p: Cut the whole head with your top length first, then step down one guard size at a time on the sides and back, blending each line as you go.
A low fade begins just above the ears, a mid fade about halfway up the sides and a high fade near the temple line. Say your top is a #3.

With a #2, cut the sides and back up to a little below where the top length starts, flicking the clipper outward at the end of each upward pass. Then use a #1 for a lower band, and a #0.5 or the open taper lever for the lowest band near the ears and nape.

Each guard change leaves a visible line. Soften it with half sizes or the taper lever, using a scooping motion that pulls the clipper away from the head as it rises. Small, gentle passes beat big ones; you can always take more.

Use landmarks such as the top of the ear, the temple corner and the occipital bone at the back of the skull. Check symmetry from the front. If one side ends up higher, raise the other to match. Skin fades finished with a foil shaver look sharp but need weekly upkeep.

sections.h: How Often Should You Trim a Buzz Cut, and How Do You Grow It Out?

blocks.p: Hair grows about half an inch a month, roughly 1 to 1.5 cm, so a buzz changes visibly within a week or two. Trim a #1 or #2 every 7 to 10 days and a #3 or #4 every two to three weeks. Fades and line-ups lose their edge first, so give them a quick trimmer pass between full cuts.

Your scalp is now the hairstyle. Wash it regularly with a gentle shampoo, since short hair hides no oil or flakes. For dandruff, a medicated shampoo with zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole helps. Use a light, fragrance-free moisturizer if your scalp gets tight in winter, and a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen or a hat for long stretches outdoors.
A neat buzz with an overgrown neck or shaggy sideburns undoes the effect. Trim both every time you cut.

From a #1 or #2, expect about two months to a short, styleable crop, four to six months to a classic short cut, and nine months to a year or more for hair you can push back or part. The awkward stage usually hits around six to ten weeks. Keep the sides and back trimmed to a #2 or #3 every few weeks while only the top grows, and use a little matte paste or clay on cowlicks once you have about an inch on top.

mistakes: Going straight to a #1 on your first buzz leaves no room to adjust if your head shape or scalp surprises you. Start at a #3, live with it for a few days, then step down. Shorter is a minute away; longer is weeks away.
Wet hair clumps and lies flat so the clipper skips strands, and oily hair clogs the guard. Wash and fully dry your hair, comb it upward and the cut comes out even in one session instead of patchy.
Pressing the Guard Into the Scalp

Pushing hard tilts the guard and cuts some spots shorter than others, especially at the crown. Hold the clipper flat with light pressure and move slowly so the guard lifts and feeds the hair. Cover each area twice from different directions.

Squaring the front hairline looks crisp for a week, but pushing it back makes a receding hairline look worse and takes weeks to regrow. Follow your natural line and only clean up stray hairs below it.
A short buzz exposes skin that has spent years under hair, and it burns quickly. Use an SPF 30 or higher spray or light lotion on sunny days, or wear a hat for long periods outdoors.
bottomLine: A buzz cut is one short, even length cut with clippers and a guard, and the guard number is the whole decision. Use the chart, then adjust one guard after you see the result: a #3 is the safe first cut, a #2 the classic, and a #1 or shorter the sharpest look and the best for thinning hair. Check your head shape and hairline before going very short, add a fade and a tidy neckline if you want it to look barber-finished, and trim every one to three weeks. Keep the clipper clean and oiled, cut on a hard floor that sweeps up easily, and protect your newly exposed scalp from the sun.

faqs.a: A buzz cut is a short haircut where all the hair is clipped to one even length using electric clippers and a numbered guard, usually #1 to #4. That leaves about 3 to 13 millimeters of hair. It needs no styling, takes about ten minutes and is easy to maintain at home.

faqs.q: What number is a standard buzz cut?
faqs.a: A #2 guard, which leaves about 1/4 inch or 6 mm, is the standard buzz cut. A #1 at about 3 mm is shorter and sharper, and a #3 at about 10 mm is a softer buzz that shows less scalp. Guard lengths vary slightly by brand, so stay with one brand's guards.

faqs.q: What is considered a buzz cut by a barber?
faqs.a: Barbers generally consider a buzz cut any clipper cut with a guard where the top is #4 or shorter, roughly half an inch or less. Pure buzz cuts are the same length all over. When the top is longer and the sides taper shorter, most barbers call it a crew cut instead.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a buzz cut and a crew cut?
faqs.a: A buzz cut is usually one uniform length all over, cut with a single guard. A crew cut keeps the top longer, often #4 to #6, and takes the sides and back shorter with a taper or fade. A crew cut is more forgiving of head shape, while a buzz is simpler to maintain.

faqs.q: Will a buzz cut suit me?
faqs.a: A buzz cut suits you if your head has no strong flat spots or ridges and you are comfortable showing your scalp and hairline. Check your head in two mirrors, then start with a #3, which flatters most shapes. Square and oval faces suit very short cuts; round faces often look better with faded sides.

faqs.q: How long does a buzz cut take to grow back?
faqs.a: Hair grows about half an inch a month. From a #1 or #2, expect about two months to a short crop you can style a little, four to six months to a classic short haircut, and nine months to a year for longer styles. Trim the sides while the top grows to skip the awkward stage.

faqs.q: How often should you trim a buzz cut?
faqs.a: Trim a #1 or #2 buzz cut every 7 to 10 days to keep it crisp, and a #3 or #4 every two to three weeks. Fades and line-ups lose definition fastest, so touch them up with a trimmer between full cuts. Tidy the neckline and sideburns every time.
